translations.text: On the fifth day of the month of March. The martyrdom of Saint Basiliscus. At that time, when Maximian was emperor,
another governor named Agrippa came as successor in place of Asclepiodotus.
He went to the eastern region to bring in the Christians, ordering them to sacrifice to the gods. Blessed Basiliscus was in prison,
weeping and praying and saying, “Lord, remember me and make my calling manifest,
so that I may not be separated from the holy men.” And the Lord appeared to him and said, “I have remembered you.
I have written your name with the martyrs who were with you before.
You have grieved because you were called later, but you will be greater than many.
Go, however, and settle your affairs with your relatives. Then you will come and suffer martyrdom in Comana.
But do not be afraid of the torments, for I am with you, and fear of men will not harm you.”
After praying, Basiliscus saw the prison doors open. When [?] daylight came, he rose and pleaded with the soldiers guarding him,
saying to them, “Give me leave for a few days, so that I may go and make arrangements for my relatives
in the village of Chumiana. Afterward I will come to my true kinsman,
my Lord Jesus Christ.” But the soldiers said, “We are afraid that they may soon begin looking for you.”
Basiliscus said, “Then let us go together, my brothers, before the governor comes to Comana.”
So the soldiers went with Saint Basiliscus, and when they arrived, they stayed with him in his house.
When he saw his brothers and his mother, he pleaded with them, saying, “Remain steadfast in the faith of Christ,
and pray to the Lord for me, that I may reach my end in this confession of faith.
For I am leaving you, and from now on you will not see me in the flesh. When I have gone
to the Lord, I will pray for you and for all Christian people, so that idol worship among the ungodly may now cease
and the grace of Christ may come throughout the whole earth.” Meanwhile, the governor Agrippa entered the city of Amasea
and summoned the elders of the city. There had long been an idol temple called Petasus,
and another called Seraphim. After offering a sacrifice near it, he then sought Basiliscus
and ordered that he and the other prisoners be brought to the city of Comana and tried there.
For he wished to leave Amasea quickly. The governor said to the magistrian and the soldiers,
“Bind Basiliscus and bring him, beating him as you go.” So they went and seized Saint Basiliscus.
And after binding him, they made him a shoe and drove sharp nails into the shoe.
They put it on him and drove him along, beating him, so that his blood drenched the ground.
For the nails penetrated to his bones. Such were the strict orders given to those sent to him by the governor.
As Christ’s martyr was being led to Comana, suffering great torment, the saint began to sing, saying:
“Though an army encamp against me, my heart will not be afraid. The Lord is my helper,
and I shall look upon my enemies. O Lord my God, save me from the mouths of lions,
and preserve me with your saints.” While he was praying, they reached a village to rest a little.
The mistress of that village was a pagan woman named Troiana.
She entertained the men who were leading Saint Basiliscus; there were about thirteen of them.
While they were eating in a room, they tied the saint to a dry sycamore tree.
Being bound once again, he prayed at length, and a crowd gathered around him.
Immediately there was a tremor and a ringing sound, so that those escorting him sprang up in fear.
When the crowd came to him, they all marveled to see that the tree had put forth leaves.
For they knew that it had long been dry, and a spring flowed out of it.
It remains to this day. When the crowd saw the Lord’s miracles, they pushed one another,
each trying to be the first to touch him. When the mistress of that village saw the miracle that had taken place,
she believed in the Lord with her entire household. They also brought people possessed by demons to him,
and they were healed. He performed many other signs as well, and everyone glorified God.
The governor’s servants also believed in the Lord and released him from his bonds.
Immediately a herd of oxen came down from the mountain and bowed before him. As they continued along the road,
signs occurred everywhere through Saint Basiliscus, as he prayed and said:
“In all his places my soul will bless the Lord.” When they arrived at a certain village, they wanted to eat.
They said to him, “Eat, for this is the third day since you have tasted anything.”
But the blessed man said, “I am filled with immortal food. Bread nourishes you,
but the word of God nourishes me. Wine gladdens you, but the grace of the Holy Spirit gladdens me. Food strengthens you, but Christ strengthens me.”
Meat will satisfy you, but prayers will satisfy me. Earthly things give you rest, but my Christ gives me rest. Robes will clothe you,
but righteousness will clothe me. You delight in laughter, but I in singing. You adorn yourselves with gold,
but I with the cross. You hope to see a ruler whose reign is brief, but I hope to see the eternal King.
For my Lord will say, “Come, you who are blessed by my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you.”
When they arrived in Comana the next morning, they heard from many people about the tortures the governor was inflicting
on the Christians. The imperial officer went in to the governor and said, “Basiliscus has arrived.”
The governor ordered that he be brought into the temple of Apollo to offer sacrifice. But if he was unwilling,
he was to be put to death at once. They led him out and beat him, saying, “Go into the temple and sacrifice.
For the governor has ordered that you either sacrifice and escape punishment, or refuse to sacrifice and die a miserable death.
Think carefully, then, so that you do not die a miserable death by believing in an invisible God.”
The holy martyr said, “I know that my God is always visible, and he sees those who are worthy of him.
For my part, I will remain silent. Let those who escorted me tell of the miracles of my God that they saw on the way.”
The soldiers who had been with him said, “Truly, we saw great miracles as we traveled with him.”
While they were saying this, men came, took Basiliscus, and brought him before the governor.
The governor said to him, “Are you the one known as Basiliscus?” He replied, “I am.”
The governor said, “Why, then, do you not offer sacrifice as the emperor commands?” Basiliscus said, “Who told you that I do not offer sacrifice?
I always offer my God a sacrifice of praise.”
When the governor heard this, he was glad and said, “Thanks be to the merciful gods!” And approaching
the sacrificial pyre, Basiliscus said to the priests, “What is the name of your god?” They said, “Apollo.”
Basiliscus said, “The name of your god signifies destruction for those who believe in him.
For everyone who believes in him will perish forever.”
The governor said, “What is the name of the God to whom you said you offer sacrifice?”
Basiliscus said, “My God is inexpressible and incomprehensible,
beyond understanding and description, being invisible.” The governor said, “What, then? Does the God to whom you say you offer sacrifice have no name?”
Basiliscus said, “If you command it, I will speak the names of my God that are set down in the holy books.”
The governor said, “Speak without fear.” Basiliscus said, “He is called Father and Almighty,
and Lord and God and King of all, and Lord of hosts, and Savior,
and compassionate and generous and merciful and patient. To him I offer
a sacrifice of praise.” The governor said, “Just sacrifice to whichever god you wish, and spare us.
For you were not summoned to act clever.” Basiliscus said, “Pay attention to my sacrifice.”
And raising his hands to heaven, he said, “Almighty God, you alone are good and compassionate.
You listen to all who serve you in truth. Show your goodness also toward me, your unworthy
servant, you who made humanity and shaped it in your holy image,
who breathed your Holy Spirit into us. Lord Jesus Christ, hear my voice,
and shake this unfeeling and deaf idol, and cast it down and shatter it.
Scatter their foul sacrifice, and show them that you alone are God.
Reveal through me the power of your divinity at this very hour.” And immediately, when he had offered this prayer,
fire came down from heaven and burned up the temple, and reduced the falsely named god to fine sand.
When the governor saw this, he fled outside, and the whole city was thrown into turmoil by the terror that had come upon them.
But the saint remained inside, singing and saying, “Let God arise, and let his enemies be scattered,
and let those who hate him flee from his presence. Let fire go before him
and burn up his enemies all around.” The governor ordered soldiers to be sent to bring him out of the temple,
for he was fiercely gnashing his teeth at him. And he said to him, “You fool,
a stranger to all the gods’ mercy! Why did you say one thing and do another? You said you would sacrifice,
but instead of a sacrifice, you brought fire upon the temple through your sorcery and burned up our god.
If you were not a sorcerer, that fire would have burned us too, had we not escaped, and it would have burned you too, since you remained inside.
Yet you remained unharmed, though you were inside amid the fire.
But now confess your sorcery to me, and come forward and sacrifice, and I will release you. But if you refuse,
I will put you to death outright.” Basiliscus said, “I do not sacrifice to lifeless idols, but to my God,
who is in heaven, I offer a sacrifice of praise. And as for the signs of fire that you saw, I will perform others greater than these.”
In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. The commander became angry and ordered him to be beheaded.
They led him out of the city and beheaded him at a place called Dioscorus.
The commander ordered his body to be thrown into the river, but the Christians took it from the executioner,
giving him thirty gold coins. And a certain Christian named Marinus built a church for him in Comana.
Many miracles take place at that place, and all who enjoy the miracles
glorify the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, now and always and forever and ever. Amen.
